t: RLE Iterator — Skip Through Runs with a Pointer
o: We must simulate consuming elements of the decoded sequence without ever materializing it. Each pair `(count, value)` in `encoding` describes a run; `next(n)` consumes `n` items and returns the value of the last consumed item, or `-1` if we run out mid-consumption. In Example 1, `[3,8,0,9,2,5]` decodes to `[8,8,8,5,5]`: `next(2)` eats two 8s (return 8), `next(1)` eats the last 8 (return 8), `next(1)` eats one 5 (return 5), and `next(2)` fails after eating the final 5, so it returns -1. Constraints are tiny (≤1000 pairs, ≤1000 calls), but counts and n can be up to $10^9$, so any approach that expands runs into individual elements is impossible — we must skip whole runs arithmetically.
k: Never expand runs: consume them in bulk by subtracting run lengths from n.
A single pointer to the current pair suffices; exhausted pairs can be skipped permanently.
If remaining n exceeds all remaining counts during a call, return -1 immediately.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force with an Expanded Queue
a.i: Decode the array into an actual list/queue of values at construction time, then `next(n)` pops n values. This directly mirrors the problem statement but is infeasible for large counts since encoding[i] and n can be up to $10^9$; it only works conceptually or when inputs are small. Included as the intuitive baseline.
s: In the constructor, build a list by appending each value count times.
For next(n): if fewer than n elements remain, drain everything and return -1.
Otherwise pop n elements and return the last popped value.
a.t: O(total decoded length) time and memory — explodes for counts up to $10^9$.
a.sp: O(total decoded length) for the expanded queue.

a.i: Keep a pointer `idx` to the current pair. For `next(n)`, repeatedly subtract the current run's remaining count from n and advance past exhausted runs; if n hits zero exactly at some point, the answer is that run's value. If we fall off the end of the array while n is still positive, return -1. Each call advances the pointer monotonically, so total work across all calls is O(len(encoding)).
s: Store the encoding and set idx = 0.
While n > 0: if idx is past the array, return -1.
Let cnt = encoding[idx]. If cnt >= n, decrease encoding[idx] by n and return encoding[idx+1].
Otherwise subtract cnt from n and advance idx by 2.
The loop terminates because each iteration either returns or consumes a whole run.
a.t: Amortized O(1) per call, O(m) total where m = number of pairs, since idx only moves forward.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the input array (we mutate counts in place).

w: Always present Approach 2 in an interview; mention the brute force only to justify why expansion fails given counts up to $10^9$. Pitfalls: forgetting zero-count runs (they're skipped naturally by the loop), returning the wrong value when n exactly exhausts a run (must return that run's value before advancing), and integer overflow in C++/Java if you precompute totals — avoidable here since we never sum counts. Edge cases: exhausting the last element exactly, calls after exhaustion (keep returning -1), and n larger than all remaining elements. Follow-ups: support peek() (look at current run's value without consuming), implement as a true iterator protocol, or handle a stream of encoded data where you cannot store the whole array (same pointer logic works streaming).
